morseCode.tapKeyHint: A short press is a dot, a long press (3x a dot) is a dash. A short pause ends the letter, a longer pause ends the word. You can also focus the key and use the space bar. Lower the WPM if it feels too fast.

korean.title: Korean Morse code (SKATS)
items: Korean Morse code assigns one code to each of 14 consonants and 12 vowels; each syllable is split into jamo and sent in order. Example: 사랑 = ㅅ ㅏ ㄹ ㅏ ㅇ
Tense consonants are sent as the same consonant twice (ㄲ = ㄱ ㄱ), compound vowels as their parts (ㅘ = ㅗ ㅏ, ㅢ = ㅡ ㅣ, ㅒ = ㅑ ㅣ, ㅖ = ㅕ ㅣ), and final clusters as two consonants (ㄳ = ㄱ ㅅ).
Korean codes overlap with Latin ones (ㅏ = E, ㄱ = L), so choose 'Korean' when decoding. Digits and punctuation use the international codes.
Syllable boundaries are not transmitted, so the decoder attaches final consonants first (먹고, 있습니다). A tense consonant between vowels, as in 아까, may read back as 악가.

basics.title: Basic Rules
items: Dot (·) = 1 unit, dash (−) = 3 units. The gap between dots and dashes within a letter is 1 unit.
Between letters = 3 units (type a single space)
Between words = 7 units (type / or three spaces / a new line)
Speed (WPM) is how many times 'PARIS' (50 units) is sent per minute. 1 unit = 1.2 ÷ WPM seconds (60 ms at 20 WPM).

tips.title: Tips
items: SOS (··· −−− ···) is really one continuous distress signal sent without letter gaps. You can send the same rhythm with a flashlight or whistle.
Don't count dots and dashes — learn each letter as a sound rhythm. 18–20 WPM character speed with a 5–10 WPM effective speed is a great start.
Tap any cell in the code table to hear that character.
Vibration only works in browsers that support the Vibration API, such as Android Chrome (not iPhone Safari).
WAV files make great props for escape rooms, quizzes and video sound effects.

whatIs.title: What is the Morse Code Converter?
whatIs.description: The Morse code converter turns text into international (ITU) Morse code and decodes Morse back into text. It covers letters, digits, punctuation and prosigns, plus Korean Morse code (SKATS), which is encoded jamo by jamo and reassembled into syllables when decoding. Adjust the character speed (WPM), Farnsworth effective speed and tone; the code being played is highlighted and also shown as a light or vibration signal. Save the audio as a WAV file, tap Morse out with a straight key, or learn it with Koch-method listening practice.

howToUse.title: How to Use
items: 1. In 'Text → Morse', type Latin, Korean or digits and the Morse code appears instantly. Check each character under 'Character by character'.
2. In 'Morse → Text', enter dots (.) and dashes (-) with a space between letters and / between words. For Korean Morse, switch 'Decode as' to Korean.
3. Press Play to hear it; the current code is highlighted and also shown as a light signal or vibration (on supported devices). Use the sliders for character speed, effective speed and tone.
4. 'Save WAV' downloads the audio; Share or Copy link sends your exact input and settings.
5. Tap the straight key short/long to send by hand, and use the 'Listening practice' tab to copy random letters and build speed.

items.q: What is SOS in Morse code?
items.a: SOS is ··· −−− ···. It was never three separate letters but one continuous signal (a prosign); 'Save Our Souls' is a later backronym. It was chosen as the international distress signal because its rhythm is simple to send and recognize.

items.q: Can Korean (Hangul) be converted to Morse code?
items.a: Yes. Korean is converted jamo by jamo using the Korean Morse table (SKATS); for example 사랑해 is sent as ㅅ ㅏ ㄹ ㅏ ㅇ ㅎ ㅐ. Korean codes overlap with Latin ones, so set 'Decode as' to Korean when decoding to reassemble the jamo into syllables.

items.q: How are dots, dashes and separators entered?
items.a: Dots can be . · • and dashes - − _. Separate letters with one space and words with / or three spaces / a new line. You can also tap them out with the straight key button.

items.q: What are WPM and Farnsworth speed?
items.a: WPM is how many times the standard word 'PARIS' is sent per minute. Farnsworth timing sends each character at the faster character speed but stretches the gaps between characters and words to lower the overall (effective) speed, using the ARRL formula.

Start by copying just two letters (K and M) at full speed. Once you're above 90% accuracy, add one letter at a time until you know all 40. The 'Listening practice' tab supports both the Latin Koch order and Korean jamo.
